R3-W1-ACCESS-METHOD.latex:
\noindent\textbf{Equal-budget control.} Retrospectively, every Access
first request on the primary holdout is multiplied by
$k=\sum_t\hat y_t^{\mathrm{CAMP}}/\sum_t\hat y_t^{\mathrm{Access}}$.
Scaling uses requests alone; predictions, histories, peaks, and the runtime
convention remain fixed. We compare underallocations and recorded unused
memory-time.

R3-W1-SIZEY-METHOD.latex:
\noindent\textbf{Matched operating points.} We apply the equal-budget rule
to Sizey. We also compare total requests across all tasks after applying each method's
smallest uniform multiplier achieving at least 95\% observed coverage.

R3-W1-ACCESS-RESULT.latex:
\noindent\textbf{Equal-budget comparison.} Scaling Access by 1.315 matches
\toolname{}'s 34,277.55~GiB budget and yields 2 underallocations versus
\toolname{}'s 31.
\toolname{} uses 39.87 versus 143.19~GiB-hours of recorded unused memory-time
(72.2\% less), showing a coverage--memory-time tradeoff.

R3-W1-SIZEY-RESULT.latex:
\noindent\textbf{Matched operating-point comparison.} Scaling Sizey by
2.2546 matches \toolname{}'s 79,049.42~GiB budget. \toolname{} underallocates
287 tasks versus 1,119 (74.4\% fewer). At 95.004\% coverage (1,066
underallocations each), \toolname{} requests 77,818.52 versus
93,357.81~GiB (16.6\% less). These operating points show fewer
underallocations at equal budget and less memory at matched coverage.
